1338.title: Yud
1338.hook: the smallest letter, which begins God's name
1338.howItsDone: Jews traditionally do not pronounce God's holy name as written: in prayer and Torah reading it is read as Adonai, and in everyday speech some say Hashem, 'the Name'. Scribes writing a Torah scroll must form every letter, even the tiny yud, correctly.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the week with tov, good, said over the first light. Your line: tet for good. A new week starts with a very small letter.

On a page of Hebrew, the letters sit on the line and fill the space between top and bottom. One doesn't. It hangs from the top line like a drop of water that hasn't fallen yet: a short stroke, a little hook, hardly more than a comma. You could miss it. A scribe writing a Torah scroll can't. And this tiny mark has a double life. It begins a word scribes treat with special care, the name of God. And it's the hero of a tender story the rabbis tell, about a letter that went missing and wouldn't stop asking to be used.
screen: `A DROP HANGING FROM THE LINE.` → `EASY TO MISS.` → `IT BEGINS GOD'S NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the name. The holy name of God in the Torah, which the King James renders LORD in capital letters, begins with a yud. Jewish tradition treats that name with such care that it isn't spoken aloud as written. In prayer and Torah reading, Jews traditionally say Adonai, my Lord, in its place, and in ordinary talk some say Hashem, the Name. So the smallest letter stands at the front of the word held with such care. Second, a story. Remember Sarai becoming Sarah? The yud at the end of her name came off to make room. The rabbis, in the Jerusalem Talmud, imagine what happened to it. The little yud came before God and complained: I was in the name of a righteous woman, and now I've been taken out. It kept asking, for a long time, until God placed it at the front of another name. In Numbers, Moses sends scouts into the land and renames one of them. In the King James: "And Moses called Oshea the son of Nun Jehoshua." Hoshea becomes Yehoshua, Joshua. A yud added to the front. The lost letter found its place. Third, why tell it. It's a story about something small refusing to be wasted; the rabbis wouldn't let even one letter fall off the page and be forgotten. A lot of any day is yud-sized: a text answered, a dish washed, a name remembered. Small isn't the same as unimportant.

segments.voice: Pick something tiny you'll do today anyway: making the bed, pouring a glass of water, folding one shirt. In your mind, do it slowly and completely, the way a scribe forms a yud, the whole of your attention on something nobody else may ever notice; if you pray, offer that small act as part of your prayer.
Yud. The smallest letter, which begins God's holy name, and in the rabbis' story moved from Sarai's name to Joshua's. Today's word.

1339.title: Kaf
1339.hook: kaf is a palm of the hand
1339.howItsDone: Some families sing Eshet Chayil, the poem from the end of Proverbs that includes 'she stretcheth out her hand to the poor', at the Friday night Sabbath table; children learning the alef-bet may meet kaf as the palm of a hand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the smallest letter, the yud that begins God's name and found its way into Joshua's. Your line: the smallest. Today, a letter you can hold in your hand.

Hold out one hand, palm up. It's the shape of asking and the shape of offering: a beggar's hand looks like this, and so does a host's, saying come in, sit down. Now close it into a fist. Same hand, different message. Turn it palm down: covering, keeping, holding back. A hand can say a lot without a word. Hebrew has a word for the open, hollow part, the palm that can hold water or hold out bread. Today's letter carries that word as its name.
screen: `PALM UP: ASKING, OFFERING.` → `A FIST.` → `PALM DOWN: HOLDING BACK.`

segments.voice: Kaf is the word for the palm of the hand, and the Bible uses it in more than one place. Start with a bird. After the flood, Noah sends out a dove, and it comes back, because, in the King James, "the dove found no rest for the sole of her foot." In Hebrew, that sole is kaf too: the flat, open underside of a foot. So kaf is the part of you that meets the world, the palm that touches, the sole that stands. Next, a woman. The poem at the end of Proverbs, praising a woman of valor, says: "She stretcheth out her hand to the poor." The Hebrew is kappah, her palm. She doesn't just give; she opens the flat of her hand. Some families sing that poem at the Friday night table. Then, a question at the gate. Psalm twenty-four asks who may go up into the hill of the LORD, and answers: "He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart." Clean hands, kapayim, palms again: not only what the hand gives, but what it has held. Together, kaf becomes a little map of a life: where you stand, what you offer, what you've touched. And there's a plain fact of the body: a palm can't hold on and give at the same time. The fingers have to open first. Opening the hand is already half the gift.

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap and close them gently into loose fists, noticing what you might be holding on to today: a worry, a grudge, a plan gripped too tightly. Then slowly turn them over and open them, palms up, fingers relaxed, and breathe into the open space without forcing anything out. If you pray, you can pray with your palms like this.
Kaf. The palm of the hand, the sole of the foot: the open, flat part that stands, touches and gives. Today's word.
Your line: open palm. Where you stand, what you offer, what you've touched. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1340.title: Lamed
1340.hook: the tallest letter; lamad means learn
1340.howItsDone: In a beit midrash, a study hall, students may learn in pairs called chavruta, reading texts aloud and arguing over them; Torah study, talmud torah, is counted in Jewish tradition as a commandment in its own right.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kaf, the palm: the sole of the dove's foot, the hand stretched to the poor. Your line: open palm. Today, a letter that reaches up.

The room is loud. Not a library hush, the other kind. Long tables, big books open, and pairs of people leaning toward each other, arguing. One reads a line aloud. The other says, wait, that can't be right, look at this word. Someone laughs. Someone thumps the page. This is a beit midrash, a study hall, and the noise is the point: learning here is done out loud, in pairs, with someone who will push back. Over the door you could hang a single letter, sticking up above all the others.
screen: `A LOUD ROOM.` → `TWO PEOPLE, ONE BOOK.` → `THE STUDY HALL.`

segments.voice: First, look at it. The letters around it sit between two invisible lines. Lamed doesn't stay put: its neck rises above the top line, and teachers of the alef-bet call it the tallest letter. A letter reaching for something higher. Second, listen to it. Lamed opens the verb for learning. Lamad: he learned. Limed: he taught. A student is a talmid, a teacher a melamed, and the great collection of the rabbis' discussions is the Talmud. Hear the same three letters, l, m, d, in each: the student, the teacher and the book. Third, the Torah. When Moses gathers the people to repeat the commandments, in the King James he says: "Hear, O Israel, the statutes and judgments which I speak in your ears this day, that ye may learn them, and keep, and do them." Learn, then keep, then do. Learning comes first in the line, and doing comes out of it. Fourth, how learning goes wrong. In Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the sages, Hillel teaches that someone too shy to ask cannot learn, and someone too impatient cannot teach. The student has to be willing to look foolish for a moment; the teacher has to be willing to explain it again. The tall letter isn't tall because it knows everything. It's reaching. Every real question you ask is a little lamed, sticking up above the line.
screen: `A NECK ABOVE THE LINE.` · `LAMAD, TALMID, MELAMED, TALMUD.` · `LEARN, KEEP, DO.` · `THE SHY CANNOT LEARN.` · then, large: `ASK THE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you've been pretending to understand: a word you nod along to, how something works at your job, a prayer you've never looked up. Name it plainly, I don't know this yet, let any embarrassment be there, and picture asking the question out loud, the way they do in the study hall. If you pray, ask for understanding.
Lamed. The tall letter, rising above the line, carrying the root of learning: lamad, talmid, Talmud. Today's word.

1341.title: Mem
1341.howItsDone: Before drinking water, observant Jews say a short blessing, the shehakol, praising God 'by whose word all things came to be'; children learning to write Hebrew are taught the open mem and the closed final mem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tall letter and a loud room full of questions. Your line: lamed learns. Today, a letter you can drink.

Before there is light, before land, before anything has a name, there is water. That's how the Torah opens. The earth is without form, darkness lies over the deep, and, in the King James, "the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters." Water isn't made on any of the days that follow. It's simply there, waiting, at the very start of the story. And the Hebrew word for it is small and round, with a humming sound you make with closed lips: mayim. Today's letter opens it and closes it.
screen: `BEFORE THE LIGHT.` → `THE FACE OF THE WATERS.` → `MAYIM.`

segments.voice: Four sips. First, the word. Mayim is spelled mem, yud, mem: the letter at both ends, a little yud between, like water held in a cup. Second, the shape. Mem changes with where it falls. In the middle of a word it's open at the bottom, a mem you could pour out of. At the end of a word it closes into a square, sealed. Mayim uses both. Some teachers like that picture: water that flows, and water that's held. Third, a name drawn out of water. In Exodus, a baby is hidden in a basket among the reeds of the river, and Pharaoh's daughter finds him. In the King James: "And she called his name Moses: and she said, Because I drew him out of the water." In Hebrew he's Moshe, and his name begins with mem. The man who will one day lead the people through the sea begins his life lifted out of a river. Fourth, the cup in your hand. Even water gets a blessing. Before drinking it, Jews who say blessings recite a short one praising God, by whose word all things came to be. Not the blessing for wine, not the blessing for bread: a short, general one, for a plain drink. Water is easy to stop noticing. The Torah puts it on the first page, and the blessing puts a pause before every glass.
screen: `MEM, YUD, MEM.` · `OPEN MEM, CLOSED MEM.` · `DRAWN OUT OF THE WATER.` · `A BLESSING FOR A GLASS.` · then, large: `WATER, ON THE FIRST PAGE.`

Look at it first, its weight in your hand and the light in it, then take one slow sip and follow it down, and let the next one take longer. If you say blessings, this is a moment for the blessing over water; if you don't, let the glass be the whole of your attention.
Mem. The letter at both ends of mayim, water, open in the middle of a word and closed at the end. Today's word.
Your line: mem is water. Even a plain glass of water is worth noticing. Until tomorrow.

1342.title: Nun and samech (Berakhot 4b)
1342.hook: nun is missing from Ashrei, but the next verse says God upholds all who fall
1342.howItsDone: Psalm 145, called Ashrei, is part of the daily Jewish prayer services; its verses follow the alef-bet, and the Talmud in Berakhot 4b explains the missing nun verse by pointing to the samech verse that follows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mem, the letter of mayim, water, and your line: mem is water. Today, two letters the rabbis read as a pair.

Psalm one hundred forty-five is built like a ladder. Each verse begins with the next letter of the alef-bet: alef, then bet, then gimel, climbing in order. Jews know it as Ashrei, from the words said just before it in the prayer book, and it comes up again and again in the daily services. Say it slowly, and somewhere past the middle a rung is gone. After mem comes samech. There's no verse for nun. A missing letter in a prayer said that often is the kind of thing the rabbis could not leave alone.
screen: `A PSALM BUILT LETTER BY LETTER.` → `AFTER MEM, SAMECH.` → `WHERE IS NUN?`

segments.voice: The Talmud asks it in tractate Berakhot: why is there no nun in Ashrei? Rabbi Yochanan answers: because a verse that begins with nun tells of Israel's fall. He points to the prophet Amos, whose lament opens with the Hebrew word for fallen, nafelah: the maiden of Israel has fallen, and will not rise again. A psalm of praise, the Talmud suggests, did not want to open a line with that word. Then another sage, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, carries it on: even so, David returned and held them up. Look at the very next verse, the samech verse. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "The LORD upholdeth all that fall." In Hebrew it begins somech, supporting. Somech Adonai l'chol hanoflim. The verse that lifts begins with samech, and its word for the fallen, noflim, comes from the same root Amos used. So the fall isn't erased from the psalm. It's folded into the next line, already being held. The empty space where nun should be is the moment of falling, and the line that catches it is right beneath. Some readers hear a picture of how a fall should go in a community: nobody pretends it didn't happen, and nobody leaves the one who fell on the ground. All of it inside a psalm said on an ordinary morning, before the day begins.
screen: `WHY NO NUN? THE TALMUD ASKS.` · `AMOS: FALLEN, AND WILL NOT RISE.` · `THE NEXT VERSE: GOD UPHOLDS THE FALLEN.` · `THE FALL IS HELD, NOT ERASED.` · then, large: `THE LORD UPHOLDETH ALL THAT FALL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has stumbled lately: a friend who lost a job, a child who failed a test, a coworker who made a public mistake, maybe you. Don't fix it yet; just notice where they are, on the ground or halfway up, and what it would look like to be the next line under them, a message, a coffee, a word that says the fall isn't the whole story. If you pray, you can say the samech verse quietly.
Nun and samech. Nun, the missing rung in Ashrei, the letter of falling. Samech, the letter of the verse that holds up all who fall. Today's word.
Your line: nun falls, samech lifts. The fall is held, not erased. See you tomorrow.

1343.title: Samech
1343.hook: the round letter of support, samach, to lean on
1343.howItsDone: Rabbinic ordination is called semichah, after Moses laying his hands on Joshua; Jewish students learn samech as the letter of the root meaning to lean on or support.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nun and samech, the gap in Ashrei, and your line: nun falls, samech lifts. Today, samech gets a day of its own.

Moses is near the end, and he asks God for a successor, someone to go out before the people so they won't be like sheep with no shepherd. God names Joshua and tells Moses: take him, and lay your hand on him. Hand, singular. In Hebrew, yadecha, your hand. A few verses later we're told what Moses actually did. In the King James words: "And he laid his hands upon him." Hands. Both of them. He was asked for one and gave two.
screen: `MOSES ASKS FOR A SUCCESSOR.` → `LAY YOUR HAND ON HIM.` → `HE LAID BOTH HANDS.`

segments.voice: Samech. On the page it's nearly a closed circle. It makes a plain s, and its root, samach, means to lean on, to rest your weight against something. Four ways in. First, the hands. When Moses lays his hands on Joshua, the verb, vayismoch, is from that root. He isn't patting him on the head. He's leaning on him, putting his own weight on the younger man's shoulders, as if to say: what held me up now rests on you. The medieval commentator Rashi notices the change from one hand to two and says Moses did it generously, more than he was asked. Second, a name. Rabbinic ordination is still called semichah, the same word: a teacher's authority, leaned onto a student. Third, the Temple. In Leviticus, a person bringing an offering lays a hand on the animal's head before it is offered. Same verb. Some readers hear it this way: before you give something up, you lean on it and make it yours. Fourth, the shape. Some teachers read samech's closed circle as support with no gap in it, a ring that holds whatever is inside. Yesterday samech was the verse that catches the one who fell. Today it's the hand on a shoulder before anyone falls at all. Support, in Hebrew, isn't only rescue. It's leaning in early, with both hands, and letting someone feel the weight of your trust.
screen: `SAMACH: TO LEAN ON.` · `MOSES LEANS ON JOSHUA.` · `SEMICHAH: HANDS THAT PASS IT ON.` · `A ROUND LETTER WITH NO GAP.` · then, large: `AND HE LAID HIS HANDS UPON HIM.`

segments.voice: Feel what's holding you up right now, the chair, the floor, the wall at your back, and lean into it a little. Then bring to mind someone carrying something new, a first job, a new baby, a new role, a hard diagnosis, and ask what both hands would look like for them: an hour of your time, a question you actually wait to hear answered. If you pray, you can hold them in it.
Samech. The round letter whose root means to lean on, the root of semichah, the laying on of hands. Today's word.
Your line: samech supports. Both hands, not one. Go gently, and come back tomorrow.

1344.title: Ayin
1344.hook: ayin is an eye, and silent
1344.howItsDone: Jewish children learning the alef-bet are taught that ayin means an eye; the idea of ayin tovah, a good and generous eye toward others, is taught from Pirkei Avot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, samech, and Moses leaning both hands on Joshua. Your line: samech supports. Today, the end of a week of letters, and a letter that watches.

A young woman runs away into the desert. Her name is Hagar, a servant in Abraham's household, pregnant, and treated so harshly that she flees. The text finds her alone by a spring on the road to Shur. There an angel of the Lord finds her too, and asks a question almost too simple: where have you come from, and where are you going? She answers honestly: she's running. Then Hagar, the outsider, does something bold. She gives God a name. Today's letter is in it.
screen: `HAGAR RUNS INTO THE DESERT.` → `FOUND BY A SPRING.` → `SHE NAMES GOD.`

segments.voice: Ayin means an eye. It also means a spring, where water wells up out of the ground. So where the angel finds Hagar by a spring, the Hebrew says by the ayin of water. Four things to see. First, the eye. Hagar calls God El Roi, which the old Jewish Publication Society translation renders a God of seeing. Then she wonders whether she has really seen the one who sees her. The runaway in the desert is not invisible. Someone has looked at her with care. Second, the spring. The place gets a name too: a well named for the living one who sees. Some readers hear why an eye and a spring share a word: both are places where something rises from deep inside. Third, the silence. In everyday Israeli speech, ayin usually makes no sound; the vowel carries the voice. Some Jewish communities, from Yemen and elsewhere, still sound it deep in the throat. Either way, it can be present without making noise, a little like a good eye. Fourth, that good eye. In Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai asks his students to go and see the good way a person should hold to. One answers: a good eye. Ayin tovah, a way of looking at people that wishes them well. So this week ran from yud to ayin: the smallest letter, an open palm, a teacher's tall lamed, water, a fall and a lift, a hand on a shoulder, and now an eye that notices without needing to be heard.
screen: `AYIN: AN EYE, AND A SPRING.` · `HAGAR: A GOD OF SEEING.` · `A LETTER THAT MAKES NO SOUND.` · `AYIN TOVAH: A GOOD EYE.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO SEES ME.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest, open or closed, and bring to mind one person you see every day but rarely really look at: a neighbor, the person at the register, the one across the table. Picture their face clearly, notice one thing you've never noticed before, and wish them one good thing without a word. If you pray, you can bring them into it.
Ayin. An eye, and a spring of water. A letter often silent, and the first letter of ayin tovah, a good eye. Today's word.
Your line: ayin is an eye. To be seen with care is a gift, even in silence. That's a week of letters.
